source: Zollman (2007) The Communication Structure of Epistemic Communities
finding: In Bala-Goyal bandit networks of finite size, the sparse cycle learns the better action more reliably than the wheel, and the wheel more reliably than the complete graph. The complete graph is fastest.
numbers: Networks of 3-10 agents; pA=0.5, pB=0.501 (agents believe 0.499 or 0.501); cycle > wheel > complete in reliability at every size. Over all graphs up to isomorphism of size 6, 10,000 trials each: four of the five most reliable graphs are minimally connected; the five fastest are complete or 1-3 edges from complete.
quote: communities made up of less informed scientists might well be more reliable indicators of the truth
limits: Single bandit task with almost indistinguishable arms. Author says the absolute probabilities should not be taken too seriously and can be changed by altering payoffs. Never tested against a real community.
agent_relevance: Origin of the claim behind G4/S3: less information flow between attempts can raise the chance the group lands on the right answer, at the price of speed.

source: Zollman (2007) mechanism section ('inertia')
finding: Why sparse networks win: a run of bad luck is contained locally, so a few agents keep trying the better action. The same containment slows good news. Reliability is bought with speed.
numbers: After a bad draw for the A2 players, the number of agents changing strategy is about 4x higher in a highly connected network. With exactly one A2 player left, a connected network is almost 3x as likely to have zero A2 players next round. Centrality ('royal family') is not the cause: in-network degree variance is uncorrelated with success.
limits: Shown only in the simulated bandit. Based on 100 runs of the six-person complete network versus the most reliable six-person network. If the uninformative action is actually better, convergence is guaranteed and connectivity only sets the speed.
agent_relevance: Gives the mechanism G4 relies on: early wrong evidence spreads to all attempts at once. Isolation stops one unlucky sample from steering every attempt.

source: Bala and Goyal (1998) Learning from Neighbours (as described in Rosenstock et al. 2017 and Zollman 2007)
finding: Origin of the two-armed bandit network model. Zollman 2007 reports that a 'royal family' of widely connected agents is harmful in their infinite-network setting.
numbers: Numbers not read in the original paper.
limits: Original paper not opened; description taken from two papers that were read.
agent_relevance: Parent model for all later work. Its conclusion is conditional on connectivity, not a claim that more talk is always worse.

source: Rosenstock, Bruner, O'Connor (2017) In epistemic networks, is less really more? Philosophy of Science 84
finding: Main failed-robustness result. The Zollman effect (cycle success minus complete-graph success) vanishes as the better arm gets easier to tell apart.
numbers: Networks of 10, n=1000 trials per round, at least 10,000 runs per setting. Effect is 0 for pB >= 0.525 and under 2 percentage points at pB=0.51. Zollman's own value is pB=0.501. Sweep covered pB 0.501-0.7, n 1-6000, size 4-100.
quote: less connectivity can improve inquiry only in a small parameter range in which learning is especially difficult
limits: Simulation. The effect never reversed in this model, so it may exist but be too small to detect. Authors say Zollman's claim that the ordering holds for all parameters is too strong.
agent_relevance: Core boundary condition. Limiting cross-talk helps only when the task is hard to judge from few samples. On easy items it only costs time.

source: Rosenstock et al. (2017) effect of trials per round n
finding: Fewer trials per round makes the Zollman effect larger, not smaller. Small noisy samples are what sparse structure protects against.
numbers: Population 10, pB=0.51, n from 10 to 10,000: the cycle-minus-complete convergence gap is largest at low n and shrinks as n grows. Control: data points needed to converge stay about constant (n=20 converges in 20 rounds, n=100 in about 12 rounds, both about 1,200 points per agent).
limits: Model result only.
agent_relevance: Maps to small-sample, noisy attempts: when each attempt gives weak evidence, a shared early wrong signal does the most harm.

source: Rosenstock et al. (2017) effect of group size
finding: Bigger communities lose the benefit and pay a huge speed cost.
numbers: pB=0.501, n=1000. Size 100: complete network reaches the better action in 99.12% of runs vs 100% for the cycle, but the complete network needs about 20 rounds on average and the cycle about 1,977. Effect strongest for small networks (6, 10, 20).
limits: Simulation only.
agent_relevance: With many attempts the group already has enough data; isolation then wastes budget. Isolation matters most for small N, like our few-attempt scaffold.

source: Rosenstock et al. (2017) Kummerfeld-Zollman epsilon-greedy replication
finding: Kummerfeld and Zollman (2016) found a reverse effect: with exploratory agents, complete networks beat cycles. Rosenstock et al. show those network differences also shrink under wider parameters.
numbers: 8-agent networks, 1000 rounds, 50 actions per round, 100 sims per cell. eps=0.05: cycle better; eps=0.35: complete better. Raising the mean of the better action's payoff (1 to 4) or lowering its SD (9 to 3) shrinks the cycle-complete difference for both eps values.
limits: Fewer parameter values explored than for the Bala-Goyal runs.
agent_relevance: Direction depends on how much individuals explore on their own. If each attempt already explores widely, sharing helps; if attempts exploit, sharing hurts.

source: Rosenstock et al. (2017) discussion: when structure matters, and alternatives
finding: Structure matters only when inquiry is hard: similar options, few agents, little data per round. Convergence time and effect size are correlated. Some models favour more connection.
numbers: Figure 8 shows a clear correlation between slow convergence and larger Zollman effect, split into small (6-20) and large (50-100) networks. Cited counter-model: Holman and Bruner (2015), biased agents trying to sway a community, where connected networks do better; Zollman (2013) says optimal structure depends on the situation.
limits: Authors say the model-world match is loose at best and treat results as how-potentially stories.
agent_relevance: Make any isolation rule conditional on a difficulty signal, not fixed. Unconditional isolation is not supported.

source: Zollman (n.d.) Beliefs and Social Networks, handbook chapter
finding: Review of the field. Diversity of search helps, but only in hard problems. Exploration is a public good, so individuals under-explore. Sparse networks are one of several ways to keep diversity and all cost speed.
numbers: Ways to keep diversity: sparser network (Zollman 2007, 2010; Grim 2013; Wu 2023), extreme initial opinions, ignoring subcommunities (Wu 2023; Fazelpour and Steel 2022), confirmation bias (Gabriel and O'Connor 2024). Some are likely to polarize (Wu and O'Connor 2023).
limits: Narrative review with no pooled effect size. Publication year not shown in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit diversity phase in S3 followed by a controlled code merge, not permanent isolation.

source: Zollman handbook chapter: experiments on landscape search and pooling
finding: Human network experiments mostly agree that limiting information can sometimes help in landscape search, but some pooling experiments favour well-connected or small-world networks.
numbers: Landscape search: limiting information sometimes helps (Mason, Jones, Goldstone 2008; Mason and Watts 2012; Derex and Boyd 2016; Charness, Cooper, Grossman 2020; Wisdom, Song, Goldstone 2004; Goldstone et al. 2013). Jonsson, Hahn, Olsson (2015): a small-world network beat the complete network on individual and collective error. Choi, Gale, Kariv (2005): 3-person directed networks mostly Bayesian-rational.
limits: Summary only; the underlying experiments were not opened. Mason and Watts is listed here as supporting limits, but Barkoczi and Galesic (b12) say it found efficient networks better, so the summary is internally inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Human evidence is mixed in direction, which matches the strategy-by-network interaction in b12.

source: Weatherall and O'Connor (2019) Conformity in scientific networks (arXiv 1803.09905)
finding: Adding a taste for conformity to a network bandit model hurts accuracy and can create stable polarization on some network shapes.
numbers: Random connected graphs, 10,016 sims per cell. k=0: all runs reach consensus, 96% on the true action. k=0.0005: correct 96%, incorrect 4%. k=0.1: correct 55%, incorrect 44%, polarized 1%; consensus of either kind only about 16%. Stable polarization needs clique-like subgroups; cycle, wheel and complete graphs cannot hold it.
limits: Model result.
agent_relevance: Warns that when agents see peers' choices and are pulled to match, group accuracy falls. Supports blocking agents from seeing majority labels (G4, G5).

source: Barkoczi and Galesic (2016) Social learning strategies modify the effect of network structure on group performance. Nature Communications 7:13109
finding: Reconciles contradictory network results. Efficient (fast) networks win if agents copy the most common solution; inefficient (slow) networks win if agents copy the best-scoring member. Small-sample conformity wins on complex tasks, best-member copying on simple ones.
numbers: 10 network structures, rugged landscape simulations. Diameter vs performance: Pearson r = +0.83 for best-member copying (slow networks better) and r = -0.77 for conformity (fast networks better). Best-member copying drives the population to one local optimum; conformity converges slower and to several solutions.
limits: Simulation, with agent strategies fixed by the authors. Human data from Mason and Watts is reinterpreted, not re-run.
agent_relevance: Best discriminating test for the Zollman effect: it depends on whether imitation is greedy (copy best) or frequency-based. Greedy copying needs isolation; frequency-based does not.

source: Barkoczi and Galesic (2016) as rival-explanation test of Lazer and Friedman (2007) and Mason and Watts (2012)
finding: They reproduce both opposite published results in one model. Lazer and Friedman (inefficient network better) comes out with best-member copying. Mason and Watts (efficient better, human experiment, 8 networks) comes out with conformity.
numbers: Participants in Mason and Watts were more likely to copy a solution if two or three of three contacts had it, which looks frequency-dependent. Result also replicated in changing environments and in the Mason-Watts landscape (supplementary).
limits: The two original papers were not opened; reported via this paper.
agent_relevance: The contradiction in the literature is mostly an imitation-rule difference, not a flaw in either result.

source: Lazer and Friedman (2007) The network structure of exploration and exploitation
finding: Agent-based simulation: a locally connected lattice beat a fully connected network in the long run on rugged landscapes (slow spread keeps exploration alive).
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Known only through Barkoczi and Galesic (2016). Agents used best-member copying.
agent_relevance: Same direction as the Zollman effect, in a different task type (landscape search, not bandit).

source: Mason and Watts (2012) Collaborative learning in networks
finding: Human behavioural experiment on 8 network structures; efficient networks outperformed inefficient ones, the opposite of Lazer and Friedman.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Known only through Barkoczi and Galesic (2016) and the Zollman chapter, which cites it in a list of limits-can-help studies. Treat the direction as unresolved until the paper is read.
agent_relevance: A human result against the less-is-more prediction in one landscape design.

source: Derex and Boyd (2016) Partial connectivity increases cultural accumulation within groups
finding: Human experiment: partly connected groups accumulated more cultural complexity than fully connected ones (from the title).
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Title known from the reference list of Barkoczi and Galesic and the handbook chapter; paper not opened (PNAS blocked).
agent_relevance: Human evidence for the less-is-more direction in innovation tasks.

source: Mayo-Wilson, Zollman, Danks (2011) The independence thesis
finding: Argues that the reliability of individual scientists and of the group can come apart, so group-optimal behaviour can need individually suboptimal behaviour.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Known by title and from the Rosenstock paper's reference list only; content summary is from background knowledge, not verified.
agent_relevance: Backs treating agent-level best behaviour separately from group-level reliability.

source: Holman and Bruner (2015) and Grim (2009) as cited by Rosenstock et al. (2017)
finding: Holman and Bruner: with biased agents trying to sway a community, connected networks do better. Grim (2009) finds a Zollman-like effect under some structural changes.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Second-hand through Rosenstock et al.
agent_relevance: The sign of the effect flips with an adversary or a different structure.

source: Li et al. (2024) Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology (arXiv 2406.11776)
finding: First direct LLM test of the Zollman idea. Neighbour-connected debate (each agent sees only 2 others) matches or beats fully connected debate and cuts input tokens by over 40%.
numbers: GPT-3.5, MATH: fully connected +4.0% over self-consistency; sparse configs +3.0% to +7.5%; neighbour-connected about +2% over fully connected. Cost savings 14.6%, 29.2%, 41.5% at three sparse levels. GSM8K: full +4.5% over SC, sparse +3.5% to +6.5%, cost down to -43.5%. MathVista (GPT-4o): best sparse +1.2% over full, +6.4% over SC, 40.6% fewer tokens. Alignment labeling: sparse +0.5% to +1.0% (GPT-3.5), +1.1% to +1.5% (Mistral 7B); cost down 50-53%.
limits: Gains are a few percent with standard deviations of 0.5 to 4.2 points, so several are within noise. Regular graphs only. Mistral 7B too weak for MATH. Variance reduced by fixing round-1 answers.
agent_relevance: Limited cross-talk in debate-like steps is no worse than full cross-talk at lower cost; the accuracy gain itself is not firmly shown.

source: Li et al. (2024) mechanism: wrong neighbours mislead; sparse debates last longer
finding: Monte Carlo test of one agent's chance of a right answer given n reference solutions of which p are right. More references help when most are right and hurt when most are wrong. Sparse debate keeps more effective rounds before consensus.
numbers: Q(n,p) for n in {2,3,4,5}, p in {0,25,50,75,100}%, three GSM8K questions, 100 runs each. Once all agents agree, almost none changes. Sparse graphs sustain more rounds before all agree.
limits: Three questions only. Explanation is correlational.
agent_relevance: LLM version of the Zollman mechanism: an early wrong majority locks everyone in. Matches G4 (agreement is a hint).

source: Li et al. (2024) heterogeneous models: put the strong model at the hub
finding: With one strong and five weak agents, putting the strong model on a high-degree node helps more than on a low-degree node.
numbers: Harmlessness labeling, 1 GPT-3.5 + 5 Mistral 7B. Strong model at degree 5: accuracy 67.0 +/- 0.8 vs SC 64.0 (+3.0). At degree 1: 65.8 +/- 0.5 (+1.8). The degree-5 strong agent spreads knowledge in one round.
limits: Single task, one small configuration.
agent_relevance: Blanket isolation is not right if one source is known better. With one model and no known better source, isolation stays.

source: Qian et al. (2025) MacNet, Scaling LLM-based multi-agent collaboration (ICLR; arXiv 2406.07155): density and shape
finding: Density and benefit are not monotone. Mesh beat tree beat chain on average, yet irregular random topologies often beat the densest mesh. No topology wins across tasks.
numbers: Random topologies use about 51.92% less time than mesh. Wider star beat deeper tree at equal density. Chain best for software, tree best for creative writing. Authors blame information overload in dense nets and credit small-world short paths. Layer topologies changed the artifact 92.16% of the time vs 68.48% for chains.
limits: Directed acyclic graphs with a memory-control mechanism; tasks are artifact building (code, writing) scored by LLM-assisted quality. The densest-is-better average partly conflicts with the sparse-debate result; the tasks differ.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one topology; it depends on whether the step builds an artifact or votes on an answer.

source: Qian et al. (2025) MacNet: direction, scale and baselines
finding: Divergent topologies beat their reversed convergent versions. Quality follows a sigmoid in agent count and saturates near 2^4 nodes. Majority voting plateaus by about eight agents.
numbers: Reversing edges alone degraded quality. Nodes tested 2^0 to 2^6 (over a thousand agents in mesh). Majority voting added only 0.9% even with CoT or AutoGPT, plateau near eight agents. Ablating agent profiles lost 3.67% on average.
limits: Quality values in the figure were garbled in text extraction and are not reported here.
agent_relevance: Fan out fresh attempts, then merge in code; many-to-one merging by a model is worse.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) AgentPrune, Cut the crap (arXiv 2410.02506)
finding: Random removal of 10-30% of communication edges in a 4-agent GPT-3.5 debate on MMLU raised accuracy; learned pruning keeps accuracy at a fraction of the cost.
numbers: Random pruning of 10-30% of links gained up to 2.83% on MMLU. AgentPrune: comparable results at $5.6 vs $43.7, 28.1% to 72.8% token reduction when added to existing frameworks, and 3.5% to 10.8% better under two agent-based adversarial attacks.
limits: The 2.83% is a best case ('up to'). Costs are for the authors' benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Redundant messages carry no extra signal. Pruning also defends against bad agents.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate (arXiv 2502.08788)
finding: Large re-evaluation: 5 MAD methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 models. MAD rarely beats chain-of-thought or self-consistency, even at more compute. Model heterogeneity helps.
numbers: 36 configs (4 models x 9 datasets), ANOVA at 0.05: SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT in only about 15% of cases; MP no significant gain. GPT-4o-mini: SoM below CoT on all nine datasets. Heterogeneous MAD: Heter-SoM +6.4% vs SoM-average, Heter-EoT +8.2% vs EoT-average; all beat CoT-average by up to +5.8%.
limits: Win-rate is per configuration. Not about topology as such.
agent_relevance: Strong counter-evidence to trusting talk. Talking agents do not beat independent sampling and voting at equal compute, in line with G7.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key? (arXiv 2402.18272)
finding: A single agent with a good prompt equals the best discussion framework. Multi-agent discussion helps mainly when the prompt has no demonstration.
numbers: FOLIO-wiki, ChatGPT-3.5 (Table 1): single-agent accuracy ranges 70.22 to 76.09 across prompt settings and discussion frameworks range 64.13 to 77.39; with demonstration plus descriptions, single agent 76.09 vs Debate(6) 77.39. Exact pairing of columns not verified.
limits: One dataset table read; column alignment of the table is uncertain, so treat exact pairs with care.
agent_relevance: Supports G7: show the scaffold's communication beats a strong plain prompt at equal tokens.

source: Yin et al. (2023) Exchange-of-Thought: cross-model communication with four topologies (arXiv 2312.01823)
finding: Tests Memory (bus), Report (star), Relay (ring) and Debate (tree) topologies for three models. All four gain over CoT with similar results; position of the strongest model matters a little.
numbers: Math: average gains over PHP +3.04% (Memory), +3.30% (Report), +3.34% (Relay), +3.20% (Debate). Commonsense: +8.06% to +8.67% over CoT. Strong model in the centre (Report) +1%; as Debate parent +0.9%. Majority-consensus stopping beat consistent-output stopping by 4.01% to 7.56% on AQuA. Over CoT-SC(5): +3.2% GPT-3.5, +1.0% GPT-4, +1.4% Claude-2.
limits: Paradigms differ little from each other; benefit is mostly from adding other models' views (diversity), not topology.
agent_relevance: Topology details matter less than who the participants are; different models help more than shape.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) Absorbing state phase transitions in multi-agent search (arXiv 2609.38327)
finding: Derives a critical communication degree d_c above which wrong hypotheses stop spreading, then tests LLM agents. Deterministic systems match the theory; LLM agents need more links than theory predicts.
numbers: Deterministic agents: Lin's CCC 0.93, 0.97, 0.94 on three tasks; mechanism task 17% above theory on average. Theory d_c: 6.10 (synthetic), 10.90 (TCAS), 6.10 (physics). Qwen3.5-4B synthetic: Team-Auto 6.55, Team-Free 12.82, Individual-Free 13.47. Other models range roughly 6.4 to 29. With free communication, d_c rises as report rate falls (r = -0.91).
limits: No LLM beat theory with statistical clarity. Six task seeds only. Model names are as given in the paper.
agent_relevance: There is a two-sided optimum: too little communication and wrong paths are not pruned, too much and errors spread. Negative evidence must be reported to others.

source: Zheng et al. (2026): reasoning effort and temperature change the optimum
finding: Stronger reasoning and lower temperature make agents herd onto the same paths, so more links are needed for the same benefit.
numbers: Higher reasoning effort on GPT-6-luna almost always raised d_c across policies and tasks; unique literals tested fell from 25.5 to 11.3 (TCAS) and 14.2 to 8.8 (physics). Higher temperature (T=1 vs 0.2) widened candidate choice and helped communication; T=0.2 raised d_c most on mechanism discovery for GPT-5.4-Nano. Individual success was equal or better with more effort.
limits: Single model per test; effects are task-dependent.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G4: correlated, low-diversity samples remove the diversity that makes sharing useful. Keep temperature varied across fresh attempts.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? MAST (arXiv 2503.13657)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups built from 150 traces and applied to 1,600+ traces across 7 frameworks. One group is inter-agent misalignment.
numbers: Annotator agreement kappa 0.88 in final rounds; LLM-judge vs human kappa 0.77. Disobey task specification is among the most frequent (11.8% to 15.2% depending on table version in the text).
limits: Does not isolate topology.
agent_relevance: Many failures come from the talking itself, so every message link is a risk surface.

source: Hagag et al. (2026) Architecture matters for multi-agent security (arXiv 2604.23459)
finding: Empirical study of 13 multi-agent designs in 3 environments on the tradeoff between task performance and attack resistance.
numbers: Abstract only read; no results extracted.
limits: Only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Topology choice also sets attack surface.
